title: LAB — ECG Interactive Session
subtitle: Week 02 · LAB · ECG Interactive Session | 18 questions

questions.text: Which of the following correctly lists the order in which an electrical impulse travels through the normal cardiac conduction system, from first to last?
options: SA node → AV node → atrium → His bundle → right and left bundle branches → ventricle
AV node → atrium → SA node → His bundle → right and left bundle branches → ventricle
SA node → atrium → AV node → His bundle → right and left bundle branches → ventricle
SA node → atrium → His bundle → AV node → right and left bundle branches → ventricle
questions.explanation:
The correct sequence is SA node → atrium → AV node → His bundle → right and left bundle branches → ventricle, which represents the normal cardiac conduction pathway.
The SA node fires, depolarizing the atria and producing the P wave. The impulse then reaches the AV node, where it is briefly delayed. From there it enters the His bundle, splits into the right and left bundle branches, and depolarizes the ventricles, producing the QRS complex.
Option A is incorrect: it places the AV node before the atrium. Atrial depolarization occurs between SA node firing and AV node activation, so the atrium must appear before the AV node in the sequence.
Option B is incorrect: it begins at the AV node rather than the SA node. The SA node is the primary pacemaker and always initiates the impulse.
Option D is incorrect: it places the His bundle before the AV node. The His bundle exits the AV node distally and is activated only after the AV node delay.

questions.text: On a standard 12-lead ECG, when the net cardiac electrical current flows perpendicular to the positive pole of a given lead axis, what type of deflection does that lead record?
options: Isoelectric — equal positive and negative components, or a flat baseline
Positive deflection, with magnitude proportional to current strength
Negative deflection, smaller in amplitude than when current flows toward the negative pole
Biphasic deflection with a dominant initial positive component followed by a negative return
questions.explanation:
When current flows perpendicular to a lead’s axis, that lead records an isoelectric deflection, because equal components of the current travel toward each pole, canceling out.
ECG deflection depends on the angle between the net current vector and the lead axis. When current flows directly toward the positive pole, the deflection is maximally positive. When it flows directly toward the negative pole, the deflection is maximally negative. When the current travels at exactly 90° to the lead axis, equal amounts project onto the positive and negative sides, producing a net-zero (isoelectric) deflection.
Option B is incorrect: a positive deflection results when current flows toward the positive pole, not when it is perpendicular to it.
Option C is incorrect: a negative deflection results when current flows toward the negative pole. Perpendicular flow produces cancellation, not a small negative deflection.
Option D is incorrect: a biphasic deflection describes transition through the lead’s axis during depolarization. The defining result of purely perpendicular flow is isoelectric, not a biphasic shape.

questions.text: The six standard limb leads are arranged in the hexaxial reference system around the frontal plane. By how many degrees are adjacent limb leads separated from one another?
questions.explanation:
Adjacent limb leads in the hexaxial reference system are separated by 30°, dividing the frontal plane into evenly spaced 30° sectors.
The six standard limb leads (I, II, III, aVL, aVR, aVF) are arranged in the hexaxial reference diagram across the full 360° of the frontal plane. Each lead has a positive and a negative pole, giving 12 equally spaced poles in total: 360° ÷ 12 = 30° per sector. This regular spacing is what makes axis determination tractable — the perpendicular to any given lead is always exactly 90° away, or three 30° steps.
Option A is incorrect: 15° spacing would require 24 poles in the frontal plane, far more than the six-lead system provides.
Option C is incorrect: 45° spacing would place only 8 poles evenly around the frontal plane, not 12.
Option D is incorrect: 60° is the angular separation between every other limb lead (e.g., lead I to lead II), not between adjacent leads.
Slide 13 · Transcript 58:22

questions.text: A cardiology student is reviewing ECG intervals. Which of the following ranges defines a normal PR interval duration?
questions.explanation:
The normal PR interval is 120–200 ms, representing the time from the onset of atrial depolarization to the onset of ventricular depolarization.
The PR interval is measured from the beginning of the P wave to the beginning of the QRS complex. It encompasses atrial depolarization plus the physiologic conduction delay at the AV node. A PR shorter than 120 ms suggests the impulse bypassed part of the AV node (pre-excitation). A PR longer than 200 ms on every beat, while every P wave still conducts, defines first-degree AV block.
Option A is incorrect: 60–100 ms is the normal heart rate range in beats per minute, not the PR interval duration.
Option B is incorrect: 80–120 ms is below the normal lower limit; a PR under 120 ms would raise concern for a bypass tract or pre-excitation syndrome.
Option D is incorrect: values in the 200–240 ms range exceed the upper limit of normal (200 ms) and would be classified as first-degree AV block.
Slide 21 · Transcript 17:45

questions.text: A 28-year-old marathon runner presents for pre-participation screening. His resting ECG shows a regular rhythm with upright P waves in leads I and II before every QRS, at a rate of 52 beats per minute. Based on standard heart-rate classification, how should this rhythm be categorized?
questions.explanation:
A rate of 52 bpm with sinus P waves falls below the 60 bpm threshold and is classified as sinus bradycardia.
Normal sinus rhythm is defined by a rate of 60–100 bpm with sinus P waves (upright in leads I and II). Any sinus rate below 60 bpm is sinus bradycardia; any sinus rate above 100 bpm is sinus tachycardia. Conditioned endurance athletes commonly have resting rates well below 60 bpm due to increased vagal tone — physiologic sinus bradycardia, which is typically benign.
Option A is incorrect: normal sinus rhythm requires a rate of 60–100 bpm; 52 bpm falls below that threshold.
Option B is incorrect: sinus tachycardia requires a rate above 100 bpm; 52 bpm is far below that.
Option C is incorrect: junctional rhythm originates from the AV junction rather than the SA node and would not produce upright sinus P waves in leads I and II; this rhythm has clearly identified sinus P waves.
Slide 31 · Transcript 22:14

questions.text: Using the 300-divided-by-large-boxes method, a student measures 5 large boxes between consecutive R-wave peaks in lead II of an ECG. What is the approximate heart rate?
questions.explanation:
With 5 large boxes between consecutive R waves, the heart rate is 300 ÷ 5 = 60 beats per minute.
Each large box on standard ECG paper equals 200 ms (5 mm at 25 mm/s paper speed). The formula is 300 ÷ (number of large boxes between R waves). The constant 300 comes from the fact that 300 large boxes fit in one minute: 60,000 ms ÷ 200 ms per box = 300. With 5 large boxes per R-R interval: 300 ÷ 5 = 60 bpm.
Option C is incorrect: 75 bpm results from 4 large boxes (300 ÷ 4 = 75), not 5.
Option D is incorrect: 100 bpm results from 3 large boxes (300 ÷ 3 = 100), not 5.
Option A is incorrect: 50 bpm would require 6 large boxes (300 ÷ 6 = 50), not 5.
Slide 32 · Slide 36 · Transcript 24:08

questions.text: A patient’s ECG shows a regular rhythm. The distance between consecutive R-wave peaks corresponds to a cycle length of 600 ms. Using the relationship heart rate × cycle length (ms) = 60,000, what is this patient’s heart rate?
questions.explanation:
Applying HR × cycle length = 60,000: HR = 60,000 ÷ 600 ms = 100 beats per minute.
The constant 60,000 equals 60 seconds × 1,000 ms/second, which is one full minute expressed in milliseconds. Rearranging: HR = 60,000 ÷ cycle length. With a cycle length of 600 ms: 60,000 ÷ 600 = 100 bpm. This sits at the upper boundary of the normal sinus rate range.
Option A is incorrect: 60 bpm requires a cycle length of 1,000 ms (60,000 ÷ 1,000 = 60), not 600 ms.
Option B is incorrect: 75 bpm requires a cycle length of 800 ms (60,000 ÷ 800 = 75), not 600 ms.
Option D is incorrect: 120 bpm requires a cycle length of 500 ms (60,000 ÷ 500 = 120), not 600 ms.
Slide 35 · Slide 36 · Transcript 26:30

questions.text: An intern is reviewing a 12-lead ECG and wants to confirm the rhythm is sinus. Which of the following P-wave findings in the standard limb leads identifies a sinus P wave?
options: P wave positive in lead II and negative in lead I
P wave positive in both leads I and II
P wave positive in lead I and negative in lead II
P wave positive in all six standard limb leads
questions.explanation:
Normal sinus P waves must be positive in both lead I and lead II, confirming that atrial depolarization originates from the SA node and travels in the expected leftward-inferior direction.
The SA node sits in the right atrium near the superior vena cava. Depolarization spreads leftward and inferiorly across the atria, moving generally toward the positive poles of lead I (oriented leftward at 0°) and lead II (oriented inferiorly at +60°). This produces an upright P wave in both leads. A P wave negative in lead I or lead II signals depolarization spreading in an atypical direction, inconsistent with SA node origin.
Option A is incorrect: a P wave negative in lead I means atrial depolarization is moving rightward, away from lead I’s positive pole — this indicates a non-sinus atrial rhythm.
Option C is incorrect: a P wave positive in I but negative in II means depolarization is moving in an unusual superiorly directed pattern rather than the normal inferior direction produced by the SA node.
Option D is incorrect: the taught criterion for sinus rhythm requires P waves positive in leads I and II specifically; not all six limb leads need to be positive, and this overly strict criterion is not the standard definition.

questions.text: A cardiologist explains to a 68-year-old man with new palpitations that his ECG shows atrial flutter. Which of the following best characterizes the mechanism and ECG appearance of typical atrial flutter?
options: A macro-reentrant circuit around the tricuspid annulus producing saw-tooth flutter waves and a regularly irregular ventricular response
Chaotic firing from multiple atrial foci producing an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm with no identifiable discrete P waves between QRS complexes
An ectopic atrial focus firing at 250–350/min producing uniform P-wave morphology and a regular ventricular rate throughout the tracing
Focal automaticity at the pulmonary vein ostia producing a rapid regular rhythm with abnormal but uniform P-wave morphology visible in all leads
questions.explanation:
Typical atrial flutter is caused by a macro-reentrant circuit spinning around the tricuspid annulus, producing the characteristic saw-tooth flutter wave pattern and a regularly irregular ventricular response.
The reentrant wavefront circles continuously around the tricuspid annulus, depolarizing the atria at 250–350 times per minute. On the ECG, these rapid, regular atrial activations appear as saw-tooth flutter waves with no flat isoelectric return between them — most clearly visible in the inferior leads and V1. The ventricular rate depends on the AV node conduction ratio (2:1, 4:1, or variable), producing a regularly irregular pattern.
Option B is incorrect: chaotic firing from multiple foci with no discrete P waves describes atrial fibrillation, which produces an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm. Flutter has a recognizable regular saw-tooth pattern, not a fibrillatory baseline.
Option C is incorrect: an ectopic atrial focus producing uniform P waves describes atrial tachycardia. The distinction is that flutter’s atrial activity appears as a continuous saw-tooth wave, not discrete P waves with an isoelectric return between each beat.
Option D is incorrect: focal automaticity at the pulmonary veins describes the trigger mechanism for atrial fibrillation. Typical flutter’s circuit runs around the tricuspid annulus, not the pulmonary vein ostia.

questions.text: The 12-lead ECG below was recorded from a 71-year-old woman who reports three days of palpitations. Her blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and she is otherwise comfortable. What rhythm does this tracing most likely represent?
questions.explanation:
This ECG shows atrial flutter, identified by the characteristic saw-tooth flutter wave pattern most visible in the inferior leads and in lead V1.
Typical atrial flutter results from a macro-reentrant circuit spinning around the tricuspid annulus, depolarizing the atria at 250–350/min. On the surface ECG these appear as saw-tooth flutter waves — rapidly undulating deflections with no flat isoelectric return between them. The ventricular rate depends on the AV node conduction ratio; the grouping of QRS complexes here is characteristic of regularly irregular flutter with variable block.
Option A is incorrect: atrial fibrillation produces a chaotically irregular ventricular rhythm with a fine fibrillatory baseline — no organized saw-tooth waves. The saw-tooth undulations visible here are incompatible with AF.
Option B is incorrect: junctional tachycardia originates from the AV junction and produces narrow QRS complexes at a regular rate, without the saw-tooth atrial activity visible on this tracing.
Option D is incorrect: sinus tachycardia has discrete sinus P waves (positive in leads I and II) before every QRS at a single regular rate. The undulating baseline without discrete P waves here excludes sinus tachycardia.
Slide 55 · Transcript 48:17

questions.text: A 77-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department for two days of palpitations and mild dyspnea. Her ECG shows an irregularly irregular ventricular rate of 108/min with no identifiable discrete P waves; instead, there is a chaotic fibrillatory baseline between QRS complexes. Which rhythm does this ECG most likely represent?
questions.explanation:
This is atrial fibrillation (AF), defined by an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm with no distinct P waves and a chaotic fibrillatory baseline between QRS complexes.
AF results from disorganized, rapid atrial activation at 350–600/min, with no coordinated atrial contraction. Because atrial impulses arrive at the AV node randomly and at extremely high frequency, AV node conduction is also chaotic, producing the defining irregularly irregular ventricular rate. Discrete P waves are absent, replaced by a fine or coarse fibrillatory baseline. The clinical rule from this session: if the rhythm is irregularly irregular, think AF — and always look for P waves.
Option A is incorrect: sinus tachycardia is regular, with a normal sinus P wave (positive in leads I and II) before every QRS. Neither the irregularly irregular rate nor the absent P waves is consistent with sinus tachycardia.
Option C is incorrect: atrial flutter with 2:1 block produces a regular (not irregularly irregular) ventricular rate with a visible saw-tooth flutter wave pattern. This tracing shows a fibrillatory baseline, not organized flutter waves, and the rhythm is not regular.
Option D is incorrect: multifocal atrial tachycardia requires at least three distinct P-wave morphologies and typically shows discrete (though varied) P waves with discernible isoelectric intervals. No P waves of any morphology are visible here; only a fibrillatory baseline.
Slide 60 · Transcript 28:44

questions.text: A cardiology student calculates the frontal axis from a 12-lead ECG and obtains a value of +220°. Based on the standard axis quadrant classifications, how should this finding be labeled?
questions.explanation:
A frontal axis of +220° falls in the extreme axis deviation (EAD) quadrant, defined as +180° to +270°.
The frontal plane axis quadrants taught in this session are: normal (−30° to +105°), left axis deviation (−30° to −90°), right axis deviation (+105° to +180°), and extreme axis deviation (+180° to +270°). EAD — also called the “northwest” quadrant — means the net QRS vector points superiorly and rightward, opposite to the normal inferior-leftward direction. At +220°, the axis is clearly within the EAD range.
Option A is incorrect: normal axis spans −30° to +105°; +220° is far outside this range.
Option B is incorrect: left axis deviation spans −30° to −90°; while EAD is also a superiorly directed axis, +220° in the numeric convention exceeds the LAD boundary values and belongs to the EAD quadrant.
Option C is incorrect: right axis deviation spans +105° to +180°; +220° exceeds the +180° upper boundary of RAD and falls into the next quadrant.
Slide 65 · Transcript 57:06

questions.text: On a 12-lead ECG, a resident identifies that the QRS complex in lead aVL is isoelectric. Consulting the hexaxial reference system, she notes that lead II is perpendicular to aVL, and the QRS complex in lead II is net positive. Using the isoelectric lead axis method, what does this indicate about the frontal axis?
options: The axis points toward the negative pole of lead II (approximately −60°)
The axis points toward the positive pole of lead II (approximately +60°)
The axis is indeterminate because an isoelectric QRS cannot specify a direction
The axis points toward the positive pole of aVL (approximately +30°)
questions.explanation:
Because the QRS is isoelectric in aVL and net positive in the perpendicular lead II, the isoelectric lead method places the frontal axis toward the positive pole of lead II, at approximately +60°.
The isoelectric lead axis method uses four steps: (1) find the limb lead with an isoelectric QRS; (2) identify the perpendicular lead in the hexaxial system; (3) if the QRS in that perpendicular lead is net positive, the axis points toward its positive pole; (4) if net negative, toward its negative pole. Here, aVL (at −30°) is isoelectric, so the axis must be perpendicular — either at +60° (positive pole of lead II) or at −120° (negative pole of lead II). Since lead II is net positive, the axis points to +60°, which is within the normal axis range.
Option A is incorrect: the negative pole of lead II points toward −120°. That direction is chosen only if lead II shows a net negative QRS, not net positive as stated here.
Option C is incorrect: an isoelectric QRS in aVL does establish a direction — it tells you the axis is perpendicular to aVL. It is the net polarity in the perpendicular lead that determines which of the two possible poles the axis faces.
Option D is incorrect: the axis points to a pole of the perpendicular lead (lead II), not to the isoelectric lead (aVL) itself. The fact that aVL is isoelectric means the axis is perpendicular to aVL, not aligned with it.
Slide 78 · Transcript 1:13:14

questions.text: The 12-lead ECG below was recorded from a 45-year-old man during a routine annual physical. Apply the quick axis check to the QRS complexes in leads I and aVF. In which frontal axis quadrant does this place the axis?
questions.explanation:
A QRS that is net positive in both lead I and lead aVF places the frontal axis in the normal quadrant (−30° to +105°).
The quick axis check uses two leads: lead I (oriented leftward at 0°) and lead aVF (oriented inferiorly at +90°). If the QRS is positive in both, the net QRS vector is directed leftward and inferiorly — within the normal axis quadrant. This is the fastest bedside screening method before applying the more precise isoelectric lead approach.
Option B is incorrect: left axis deviation requires a QRS negative in lead II (axis more negative than −30°). A positive QRS in aVF means the axis points downward, away from the LAD quadrant.
Option C is incorrect: right axis deviation requires the QRS to be negative in lead I, meaning the vector is directed rightward. A positive lead I excludes rightward deviation.
Option D is incorrect: extreme axis deviation requires the QRS to be negative in both lead I and lead aVF, meaning the vector points superiorly and rightward. Both leads are positive here, which excludes EAD.
Slide 65 · Transcript 59:06

questions.text: The 12-lead ECG below was recorded from a 58-year-old man referred for evaluation of a bradycardic rhythm. Based on the tracing, what is the most likely conduction finding?
questions.explanation:
First-degree AV block is characterized by a PR interval consistently exceeding 200 ms on every beat, with every P wave conducting to the ventricles — exactly what this tracing shows.
The PR interval normally spans 120–200 ms. When this interval exceeds 200 ms on every beat while every P wave still conducts, the pattern is first-degree AV block (also called AV delay). On this ECG the PR measures approximately 360 ms — calculated as approximately 9 small boxes × 40 ms per small box — well beyond the upper limit of normal.
Option A is incorrect: normal sinus conduction requires a PR interval of 120–200 ms. The markedly prolonged PR on this tracing exceeds that upper limit.
Option B is incorrect: Mobitz I (Wenckebach) shows progressive PR lengthening from beat to beat until one P wave fails to conduct, then the PR resets. This tracing has a consistently prolonged PR without the beat-to-beat increase or any dropped QRS.
Option C is incorrect: Mobitz II shows a constant PR interval with sudden, unexpected non-conduction of a P wave. This tracing conducts every P wave without dropped beats, and there is no constant-then-sudden-drop pattern.
Slide 87 · Transcript 1:16:14

questions.text: The 12-lead ECG tracing below was recorded from a 66-year-old woman on telemetry. She is hemodynamically stable with no chest pain. What conduction abnormality does this tracing most likely demonstrate?
options: Sinus arrest with junctional escape beats filling each pause
Third-degree (complete) AV block with no consistent P-wave to QRS relationship
questions.explanation:
This tracing shows Mobitz I (Wenckebach) second-degree AV block: the PR interval progressively lengthens beat-to-beat until one P wave fails to conduct, then the cycle resets.
Wenckebach block results from cumulative AV nodal fatigue: each successive conducted impulse takes slightly longer to traverse the node, lengthening the PR interval until the node is refractory and one impulse is blocked — dropping a QRS. After the pause, the AV node recovers and the PR resets to its shortest value, restarting the cycle. The resulting grouped beating pattern (several beats followed by a pause) is the visual fingerprint on the rhythm strip.
Option A is incorrect: sinus arrest produces a pause with no P wave at all; Wenckebach pauses occur because a P wave is present but fails to conduct. The P waves continue marching throughout the tracing at a regular rate.
Option B is incorrect: Mobitz II has a constant PR interval on all conducted beats, then a sudden dropped QRS with no preceding PR prolongation. This tracing shows increasing PR before each dropped beat, which excludes Mobitz II.
Option D is incorrect: third-degree AV block shows no consistent relationship between P waves and QRS complexes, with the P rate and QRS rate completely independent. Here the P waves are still conducting (except for the one dropped beat per cycle), and the PR follows the cyclical Wenckebach pattern.
Slide 89 · Transcript 1:34:42

questions.text: The 12-lead ECG below was recorded from a 74-year-old man brought to the emergency department with presyncope and a heart rate of approximately 35 beats per minute. Which rhythm does this tracing most likely represent?
options: Third-degree (complete) AV block with AV dissociation
Second-degree AV block, Mobitz II, with high-grade block and slow ventricular rate
Sinus bradycardia with first-degree AV block and a prolonged PR interval
Junctional bradycardia with accelerated idioventricular escape rhythm
questions.explanation:
This tracing shows third-degree (complete) AV block: there is no relationship between the P waves and the QRS complexes, and the P rate exceeds the QRS rate.
In complete heart block, no atrial impulse conducts through the AV node to the ventricles. The atria continue firing at the sinus rate while the ventricles are maintained by a slow escape pacemaker. On the ECG, P waves and QRS complexes march completely independently: P-P intervals are regular, R-R intervals are regular, but there is no fixed PR relationship. The teaching method is to “march out” the P waves across the rhythm strip — placing them at equal intervals regardless of QRS position — which confirms they are unrelated to the QRS.
Option B is incorrect: Mobitz II has a constant PR on conducted beats, with sudden non-conducted P waves. In complete heart block, no beats conduct at all; there is no PR interval to measure because no P wave is associated with any QRS.
Option C is incorrect: sinus bradycardia with first-degree AV block has a prolonged but constant PR, and every P conducts. This tracing shows P waves and QRS complexes with no fixed relationship — complete dissociation, not a slow sinus with delayed conduction.
Option D is incorrect: junctional bradycardia with AV dissociation from an idioventricular rhythm can coexist, but the defining feature of complete heart block is that the P rate exceeds the QRS rate. The clinical presentation with presyncope at 35 bpm, P-QRS dissociation, and P rate above QRS rate identifies complete heart block specifically.
Slide 93 · Transcript 1:30:53

questions.text: A 72-year-old man with known atrial fibrillation is started on a new antiarrhythmic agent for rate control. Two days later, telemetry shows a fibrillatory atrial baseline consistent with atrial fibrillation, but his ventricular rate is perfectly regular at 38 beats per minute. He reports new lightheadedness. Which of the following best explains this ECG finding?
options: Pharmacologic conversion of atrial fibrillation to sinus bradycardia by the new medication
First-degree AV block from the medication slowing conduction and regularizing the ventricular response in AF
An accelerated junctional rhythm overriding the fibrillatory atrial activity and driving the ventricles at a fixed rate
Spontaneous cardioversion of atrial fibrillation to a regular bradycardic sinus rhythm
Complete AV block superimposed on atrial fibrillation, with the ventricles driven by a regular escape rhythm
questions.explanation:
A perfectly regular ventricular rate in a patient with an ongoing fibrillatory atrial baseline is the hallmark of complete (third-degree) AV block superimposed on atrial fibrillation.
In AF, the AV node receives disorganized atrial impulses at 350–600/min, normally producing the irregularly irregular ventricular response. When complete AV block is superimposed, no atrial impulse reaches the ventricles regardless of frequency. The ventricles are driven by their own escape pacemaker at a slow, regular rate. The key teaching point: a perfectly regular ventricular rate in a patient known to have AF should immediately raise concern for complete heart block. In this case the new medication produced excess AV nodal depression.
Option A is incorrect: if the rhythm had converted to sinus bradycardia, there would be identifiable sinus P waves (positive in leads I and II) before every QRS. The tracing still shows an irregular fibrillatory atrial baseline, not organized sinus P waves.
Option B is incorrect: first-degree AV block prolongs the PR interval but does not regularize the ventricular rate in AF. In AF there are no organized P waves to slow — first-degree block cannot convert an irregularly irregular rhythm to a regular one.
Option C is incorrect: an accelerated junctional rhythm could potentially drive the ventricles at a regular rate, but a rate of 38 bpm is far too slow for an accelerated junctional focus. Moreover, junctional firing does not explain the persisting fibrillatory atrial baseline alongside a regular ventricular rate — complete AV block is the more direct and coherent explanation.
Option D is incorrect: spontaneous cardioversion to sinus rhythm would produce an identifiable sinus P wave before each QRS. The ongoing fibrillatory atrial baseline excludes sinus rhythm as the mechanism.
Slide 99 · Transcript 1:47:08
